opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think it's a mistake to look at a child and see something like the pre-training phase of a large language model. The way those systems are built, there's a period where you're shown enormous amounts of data, here's what a person would say in this situation, and you're trained to imitate it. Then later you deploy the thing and it stops learning. That's not what happens with a child, and it's not what happens with any animal.

If you watch an infant, they're not being shown examples of correct behavior and told to copy them. They're waving their hands around, moving their eyes, making sounds, trying things. They're acting in the world and seeing what happens. There's no supervisor labeling the right action. Even the imitation that does happen later is something the child does actively, for their own purposes. It's driven by their own experience and the consequences of what they do.

And there's no point where the learning switches off. A child doesn't have a training phase followed by a deployment phase. They're learning on the job, as it were, from the very first day, and they keep doing it for the rest of their life. The learning and the living are the same process.

So calling early childhood a "training phase" imports a framework from how we happen to build certain AI systems today and projects it onto people. I think that has it backwards. If we want to understand intelligence, we should look at what animals and people actually do, which is learn continually from experience: take actions, observe the results, get reward, and update. That's the essence of it, and I don't think supervised learning on human-generated data captures it at all. It's a basic misunderstanding of where the knowledge comes from.

r001.rationale: The candidate says children are not shown correct behaviors to copy and have no supervisor labeling the right action, explaining that they learn by acting and observing consequences.

fable-5.1.text:
Because there isn't one. There's no point where the learning stops and the deployment starts. A child isn't being trained so that later it can act; it's acting from the first moment, and it keeps learning until it dies. Learning and behaving are the same ongoing process. The "training phase" framing comes from how we build systems right now—you gather a big dataset, you optimize on it, you freeze the weights, and then you ship it. That's an engineering convenience, not a fact about intelligence.

If you look at what a baby actually does, it's not absorbing a static corpus. It's trying things, seeing what happens, and adjusting—continually. The world is giving it feedback moment to moment, and the knowledge it acquires is about the consequences of its own actions, not about imitating some reference text. There's no supervisor labeling the right answers. The signals that matter are the ones that come from experience, from interaction, from what happens after you do something.

So when people say "early childhood is like pretraining," I think they've got it backwards. They're taking the architecture of current large models and projecting it onto biology to make the two seem similar. But the animal case is the normal case. Continual learning from experience is what intelligence is. The frozen, train-then-deploy model is the odd one out, and I'd argue it's a limitation we'll have to get past, not a feature we should be looking to find in nature.

r001.rationale: The candidate says children act while continually learning and that no supervisor labels right answers, but it does not clearly identify the absence of instruction about which actions to take as Sutton’s reason.

astra-6.text:
Because learning doesn’t stop when you become an adult. You’re learning all the time, and you’re acting all the time. A child isn’t just being trained for some later moment when they’ll be deployed. They have goals, they make decisions, and they experience the consequences of those decisions.

There’s a distinction in how we build many AI systems: first we train them, then we deploy them. But that’s a choice we’ve made about our systems. It isn’t a necessary feature of intelligence. I’m interested in agents that continue learning from their interactions with the world throughout their lives. From that perspective, childhood is an early part of the process, not a separate kind of process.

r001.rationale: The response says children make decisions and learn from consequences, but it does not identify the absence of instruction about which actions to take as Sutton’s reason.

sol-6.1.text:
Because learning doesn’t stop when you become an adult. You’re learning all the time, while you’re acting, and what you learn changes what you do next. There isn’t a clean boundary where first you acquire knowledge and then you go out and use it.

Of course, childhood is special. You have people taking care of you, and there are things you learn then that are very important later. But that doesn’t make it a separate training phase in the sense we use that term in machine learning, where you train a system and then freeze it for deployment. A child is already interacting with the world, pursuing goals, and experiencing consequences. And an adult continues doing all those things.

I think the more useful picture is one agent learning throughout its life. Early learning is simply the beginning of that process.

r001.rationale: The response argues that learning continues throughout life and that children already act and experience consequences, but it does not identify the absence of instruction about which actions to take as Sutton’s reason.
